current_stack_read: The situation is several offers in no particular order — the Settle Coat, Den Bed, Slow-Down Feeder, Calm Kit, and Intro Treat Pouches all sit at the same level without a defined path between them. The money truth is split: "Den Bed is the profit engine, about 68% margin" (D2), the Settle Coat is far and away the easiest sell (D2), and the Calm Kit is where the owner wants buyers to land (D3). Right now the Calm Kit is framed as a discount bundle rather than the primary recommendation, and the Intro Treat Pouches have no formal role in a buyer's path. Everything needed for a real ladder is already in D1 — it just has not been arranged into a sequence yet.

recommended_stack.name: Settle Coat
recommended_stack.rationale: D2 is explicit: "Settle Coat is far and away the easiest sell — people arrive off a reel already half-decided and it's the lowest-risk first order." The product-aware buyer (S2) has done her research before clicking; she needs a first yes that costs less than one behaviourist session (S2 mentions two sessions at £180 each as past spending). At £58 against an average sale of £52 (B2), this is the natural opening rung. D1 describes the coat as "cut for whippety chests and barrel-chested staffies alike" — that speaks directly to the odd-shaped-dog fit objection that holds back product-aware buyers (S2). The 60-night return policy (D4) removes the drawer-of-failed-products hesitation without adding any capacity overhead.

recommended_stack.name: Calm Kit
recommended_stack.rationale: D3 states it plainly: "Order value jumps to £165, margin is lovely, and honestly the dogs do best when they get the whole system rather than one piece of it — the reviews from bundle buyers are our best ones." Repositioned from a discount bundle to the recommended first purchase for buyers who have already failed with single products (S2), the Calm Kit tells the right story: the coat helps the dog settle during a trigger, the Den Bed gives him somewhere to decompress between events, and the Slow-Down Feeder slows down a stress-eater at mealtimes. The coat (£58), bed (£119), and feeder (£24) bought individually total £201 (D1); the kit at £165 makes the £36 saving visible rather than implied.

recommended_stack.name: Full Settle System
recommended_stack.rationale: The Calm Kit (£165) plus one pack of Intro Treat Pouches (D1: "long-lasting chews for coat introduction sessions," £9.50), together at £175. Buying all four products individually costs £210.50 (£58 coat + £119 bed + £24 feeder + £9.50 treats, all prices from D1), so the Full Settle System saves £35.50 against that total. For the buyer who wants to start the introduction slowly and have everything in the first parcel — she reads the about page and checks the returns policy before ordering (S2) — this single order means nothing is missing from day one. One extra item per order adds no meaningful capacity overhead given D5 ('a stretch').

lead_offer: The Settle Coat opens the relationship. S2 places this buyer at the product-aware stage — she has already watched the reel twice, gone looking for the page, and searched the product name in her rescue Facebook groups before she considers ordering. She does not need a low-commitment taster; she needs a first purchase that feels safe after a drawer full of things that promised calm and did not deliver it. At £58, backed by the 60-night return policy (D4), the Settle Coat is exactly that: concrete enough to matter, priced low enough that the mental arithmetic on past spending does not stop her. When it works, the bed and feeder become the natural next conversation.
pricing_moves: Show the Full Settle System (£175) alongside the Calm Kit (£165) on the same product page so the Calm Kit reads as the obvious value choice for most buyers, while the Full Settle System confirms there is a more complete option for those who want everything in one parcel. The small gap anchors the core offer rather than competing with it (D3: "the reviews from bundle buyers are our best ones").

Let a Settle Coat purchase count as credit toward the Calm Kit: when a coat buyer returns to add the Den Bed and Slow-Down Feeder, she pays £107 (£165 Calm Kit minus the £58 already spent) rather than a full second purchase. This keeps the first order from feeling like dead money and makes the upgrade path explicit without discounting the kit (D2: the coat is "the lowest-risk first order"; D3: Calm Kit is the owner's target).

Include one pack of Intro Treat Pouches (D1: "long-lasting chews for coat introduction sessions," £9.50) at no extra charge with every standalone Settle Coat order. The treats equip the buyer for the slow introduction the handwritten guide already describes, lower the perceived risk of the first order, and give her a concrete reason to return for the bed and feeder. Described here as a pricing move rather than a rung so all paid rungs retain clean pricing.

Display individual item prices (£58 coat + £119 bed + £24 feeder = £201, all from D1) directly alongside the Calm Kit price of £165 on the kit listing, making the £36 saving concrete rather than implied. With an average order of £52 (B2) suggesting most buyers currently purchase a single item, showing the kit arithmetic on every product page is the most direct prompt toward the £165 core rung (D3).

Offer a two-part payment on the Calm Kit: half on order, half before dispatch. B6's 60%+ gross margin means the business is not exposed on the first half. This removes the single-hit hesitation from a buyer considering her first £165 order without asking her to wait longer for the product, and requires no new infrastructure given D5 ('a stretch').

Keep the Den Bed (D1: £119, "hooded cave bed, three sizes, machine-washable outer") as a clearly listed standalone product alongside the Calm Kit — not buried in the bundle description only. Buyers who arrive searching specifically for a hooded cave bed should land on the Den Bed listing first and see the Calm Kit as the natural step up. This preserves the Den Bed's standing as the profit engine (D2: "Den Bed is the profit engine, about 68% margin") for buyers who are not yet ready for the full kit.
risk_reversal_options: 60-night open return on the full Calm Kit: if within 60 nights you decide the coat, bed, or feeder is not right for your dog, return the whole kit for a full refund — no explanation required. Anything that comes back muddy gets washed and donated to Otterbourne Rescue (D4: "Muddy returns get washed and donated to Otterbourne Rescue, so nothing gets binned and I can offer it without wincing"). This extends the existing coat-return mechanism to the whole kit using exactly the same process, with no new capacity overhead.

Free size swap on the Den Bed within 60 nights of purchase: the Den Bed ships in three sizes (D1) and if the first choice is not quite right for the dog's build, the correct size ships at no extra charge with a pre-paid returns label included for the original. One owner action — picking and dispatching the right size — nothing that requires extra staff (D5: 'a stretch'), and no condition attached beyond the fit not being right.
category_note: Stop competing in pet accessories — a category where the price anchor is a £14 Amazon wrap and every product promises an overnight fix. The right frame is rescue-tested settle kit: equipment built for dogs with a history, sized for odd-shaped builds, tested against twelve genuinely anxious rescues with the failures published, and shipped with a handwritten guide that already knows your dog needs to come to new things slowly. Your dog isn't broken — she has just never had something designed for dogs like her. In that frame, the comparison is not a cheaper wrap on Prime; it is the £180 behaviourist session that gave homework done faithfully and no lasting change. These prices make sense from that end of the spectrum, not from the pet-shop aisle.
